newsitem.title: USA: Clinton proposes $5 bln for school construction.
newsitem.headline: Clinton proposes $5 bln for school construction.

text.p: President Clinton on Friday sent Congress a bill that would provide $5 billion over four years to help states and localities rebuild America's crumbling schools, the White House announced.

"We are in the midst of a virtual epidemic of old and sick school buildings," U.S. Education Secretary Richard Riley told a press briefing. "Sixty percent of schools need at least one major repair, such as roofs, walls or heat. One third of all schools need extensive repairs or total replacement."

Under Clinton's plan, roughly $2.45 billion would go to states for issuance of tax-exempt bonds or for distribution to local districts. States would have to pledge to increase over the next four years the amount of state construction paid for with state, local and private funds, the plan says.
Another $2.45 billion would be direct grants to the 100 U.S. school districts that the General Accounting Office has determined have the greatest number of poor children.
Seventy percent of the those direct grants would be allocated based on a formula and 30 percent would be distributed competitively to the neediest school districts.

The bill would subsidize 50 percent of school construction financing costs, including bonds, certificates of participation, purchase or lease arrangements, state revolving loan funds, or others, the adminstration said.
States and localities could make their own decisions about construction projects after conducting a survey of their needs, the bill says.

The administration said funds could be used to fix or upgrade classrooms; deal with health and safety problems involving air quality, plumbing, heating and lighting; and improve access for disabled students, teachers and others.

Funds also could be used improve educational technology, like communications closets, electrical systems and power outlets; build new schools because of rising or shifting student enrollments; and create after-school learning centers, community schools and charter schools.
